Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Assessment: Known asthma with 2–3 days of increased wheeze, cough, and exertional dyspnea; poor relief with salbutamol; no sputum, fever, or chest pain reported. Likely mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation on a background of persistent asthma. Atopic background (hay fever; family history of asthma/eczema). Last structured review 2 years ago.
- Contributing factors (from DDx, consistent with transcript): 
  - Exercise-related trigger (exercise-induced bronchoconstriction may contribute; onset occurred during running).
  - Possible allergic trigger given hay fever history.
  - Potential suboptimal inhaler technique or regimen given confusion about medications and limited reliever benefit.
- Safety: Advised to attend Emergency Department if breathing worsens or if needing frequent reliever use as discussed.

Management Plan
- Increase Clenil (beclomethasone, brown preventer) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review (per clinician instruction).
- Use salbutamol (blue) inhaler as needed, up to every 2–4 hours; if needing this frequently or symptoms worsen, attend Emergency Department.
- Book face-to-face GP appointment within the next few days for chest examination and peak flow measurement.
- In-person assessment may consider antibiotics and/or oral steroids depending on findings (per clinician discussion).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation on background of persistent asthma — High likelihood. Justified by acute wheeze, cough, exertional dyspnea over 2–3 days in known asthmatic with atopic background and increased reliever use with poor relief.
- Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction — Moderate likelihood. Symptoms first noticed during running and recur with brisk walking, common in asthmatics.
- Allergic asthma flare — Moderate likelihood. Atopic history (hay fever; family atopy) could predispose, though no explicit current allergen exposure reported.
